name: Mesopotamian religion
areas: the first city-states, each with its patron god
Marduk of Babylon raised to supremacy by Hammurabi
the old gods fade as Christianity spreads
Ashur, god of the city of Assur and king of Assyria
temples to the old gods into the 4th century CE
worship conducted in Ashur's name across the Assyrian domain
routes: Sargon of Akkad unites Mesopotamia; Sumerian and Akkadian gods merge (c. 2335 BCE)
Ashur's worship carried west across the Assyrian domain
marks: One of the first Sumerian city-states; with the invention of writing around 3500 BCE comes the first evidence of Mesopotamian religion.
A 5,000-year-old cultic area dedicated to Ningirsu, with more than 300 broken ceremonial cups, bowls and jars, was found here (announced 2020).
A Sumerian list of about 560 deities from here and Fara, of about 2600 BCE, ranks five gods above the rest.
The city of the god Ashur, who alone bore the title of king; its ruler was his high priest and only “steward of Assur”.
King Hammurabi raised Babylon's god Marduk to supremacy beside Anu and Enlil (18th century BCE).
Temples to Ashur, Sin, Shamash, Hadad, Bel and Ishtar were still dedicated in Assyrian vassal states up to the 4th century CE.
notes: With writing, around 3500 BCE, comes the first evidence of a Mesopotamian religion: the worship of the forces of nature as providers of sustenance, in the city-states of Sumer.
In the 3rd millennium BCE the powers of nature are personified as gods with their own functions; a list of about 2600 BCE ranks some 560 deities.
Sargon of Akkad unites Mesopotamia around 2335 BCE; Sumerian and Akkadian gods are increasingly identified with one another.
Hammurabi of Babylon raises Marduk to supremacy beside Anu and Enlil in southern Mesopotamia (18th century BCE).
In the 2nd and 1st millennia BCE each state's national god heads its pantheon; Ashur, god of the city of Assur, becomes overlord of the Assyrian domain and is worshipped across it.
The Achaemenid Persians conquer Mesopotamia (539 BCE) but do not interfere with its religion; Alexander the Great takes the region in 330 BCE.
Under the Parthians a revival in Assyria dedicates temples once more to Ashur, Sin, Shamash, Hadad, Bel and Ishtar (2nd century BCE to 4th century CE).
Christianity, introduced from the 2nd century CE, spreads among the Assyrians, and Assyria becomes a centre of the Church of the East.
By about 400–500 CE the old religion has almost completely died out, its people having largely become Syriac Christians.
src: Jean Bottéro, Religion in Ancient Mesopotamia (2001)
